CLAIM: A halted run can be safely resumed iff (1) the halt was clean—the final event was fully committed and persisted before exhaustion, leaving no partial write; (2) the resuming process can reconstitute the exact internal state at the tail of the committed event log; (3) the event log was not mutated during the pause; (4) a fresh token budget is allocated. Resumption must be refused when the halt left a partial or uncommitted event, when the log or state was externally tampered with, or when no new budget is available.

[573f12461e73] (school: school-0)
CLAIM: Resumption is safe only if the system implements an atomic checkpoint that pairs the full mutable state snapshot with the last committed event identity, and the halt occurred at such a checkpoint boundary. Without this, even a 'clean' event-level halt may hide state divergence, so resumption must be refused.
MECHANISM: The event log records discrete events, but the system's working state may include intermediate computation not yet materialized as an event. An atomic checkpoint guarantees state and event-log-tail are consistent. If the halt occurred between checkpoints, reconstructing state from the log tail may produce a different state than the runtime actually held, causing resumed events to diverge, duplicate, or skip—corrupting append-only identity through causal gaps or collisions.

[6ae711003862] (school: school-0)
CLAIM: Resumption is always safe when the system follows pure event sourcing: all state is derivable by replaying the append-only log, the last event is complete, and a write-budget guard prevented initiating any event that could not be completed within remaining tokens. Resumption is refused when the write-budget guard was absent, failed, or when the last event is incomplete.
MECHANISM: In event sourcing, the log IS the state. A write-budget guard checks remaining tokens before beginning an event write and halts cleanly if insufficient, guaranteeing no partial writes. Replay reconstructs state deterministically from the complete log. Resumption simply continues from the replayed state, appending with the next identity. The guard is the causal mechanism that makes clean halts guaranteed rather than accidental.
At formal sequence 583, artifact 6ae7110038621aa0aba62b479d39533a1b3ebd2b24e717b31d4ddf01c8a7d1c3 had formal status accepted.

[57b23d28735b] (school: school-0)
CLAIM: Resumption should always be refused; instead, a new run must be spawned that explicitly references the halted run's event log as prior context. This eliminates all corruption risk by never mutating the original log's causal stream.
MECHANISM: Even with clean halts and checkpoints, resumption conflates two causal episodes (pre-halt and post-halt) under a single run identity, risking subtle corruption from environmental drift, configuration changes, or non-determinism accumulated during the pause. A new run with a fresh identity that cites the prior log as input preserves the original log's append-only identity absolutely, while the new log's identity is independently clean. The cost is losing run-level continuity, but the benefit is eliminating an entire class of corruption modes.

MECHANISM: A pre-write reservation check creates a causal guarantee: the system never enters a state where an event write is in progress at exhaustion. This makes every halt point a safe resumption boundary by construction. Tail integrity validation on resumption detects any corruption that occurred during the pause (storage decay, external mutation). [b330eb4dbae6] (school: school-2)
CLAIM: Append-only identity corruption has two distinct senses that must be separated: (structural) the hash chain is physically broken by a torn write, and (trajectory) the chain is structurally intact but the resumed events belong to a different run trajectory than the committed prefix. A halted run can be resumed without structural corruption iff the tail event is fully committed with a finalized digest (clean halt). It can be resumed without trajectory corruption iff the system's state at the halt point is fully determined by the committed event log, including all non-deterministic inputs. Resumption must be refused for structural corruption (torn write) unconditionally, and for trajectory corruption whenever non-deterministic state was consumed but not logged—even if the chain is structurally perfect.

[009672b6c406] (school: school-2)

The key insight: resumption safety is not about how the halt happened but about whether the log is a sufficient and intact continuation point.

[04350fd6e146] (school: school-3)

[8ce8275fe2d9] (school: school-3)
CLAIM: Resumability conditions depend on the log's identity structure: with a linear hash chain, a partial write at the tail can only be detected by recomputing the entire chain (O(n)), which makes audit expensive and incentivizes blanket refusal for any uncertain halt. With a Merkle mountain range (MMR) or similar tree-structured identity, tail integrity can be verified in O(log n), and a corrupt tail event can be truncated safely by removing only the affected peak—making crash-halt resumption practical rather than prohibitively expensive, and thus changing the refusal policy from 'always refuse crash halts' to 'refuse only if audit reveals untruncatable corruption.'

CLAIM: If the underlying storage layer provides atomic append semantics (e.g., a journaling filesystem with fsync, a WAL database, or a distributed log with quorum-based commit), then the clean-halt condition is subsumed by the storage guarantee: either a full event is durably appended or nothing is, regardless of when or why the halt occurs. Under this regime, the distinction between budget halts and crash halts vanishes—both are resumable if the storage layer's atomicity guarantee holds, and resumption must be refused only when the storage guarantee itself is violated (disk failure, corruption, Byzantine storage nodes).

If the reasoning system uses non-deterministic components (e.g., external tool calls with real-world side effects), can resumption ever be truly safe, or must it always be refused in favor of a new run?

unfinished: Unresolved question

Counterfactual: Suppose the event log uses a Merkle mountain range rather than a linear hash chain. Resumption could verify log integrity in O(log n) rather than O(n). Would this change the resumability conditions? Likely not for the clean-halt requirement, but it would make tail-integrity validation cheaper, reducing the cost of the refusal-then-audit path for crash halts.
why keep: Opens the question of whether log structure influences resumability policy beyond identity preservation.
unfinished: Need to consider whether MMR-based logs change the partial-write detection semantics.

Speculative: What if the token budget itself were allocated per-event rather than globally? Each event write reserves its own budget atomically. Then exhaustion never interrupts a write—it simply prevents the next write from starting. This collapses the 'clean halt' condition into the system's normal operation, making all halts resumable by construction. The cost is tighter per-event budgeting and potential underutilization of a global pool.
why keep: This would eliminate the partial-write corruption class entirely by construction rather than by guard.
possible next move: Analyze whether per-event budget reservation is feasible under common token-accounting models (e.g., OpenAI-style token counting where output length is not known a priori).

data.problem_text: A reasoning system halts a run when its token budget is exhausted. State the precise conditions under which such a halted run can later be resumed without corrupting the append-only identity of its recorded events, and the cases in which resumption must stay refused.
